answers.solution:
An off-by-one error in a self-test for tick 210 typically manifests as a fencepost error in a loop or slice boundary. The most common culprit is using `<=` where `<` is needed (or vice versa) when iterating over 210 items.

**Before (buggy):**
```go
// Processes 211 ticks instead of 210 (indices 0..210)
for i := 0; i <= tickCount; i++ {
    processTick(i)
}
```

**After (fixed):**
```go
// Processes exactly 210 ticks (indices 0..209)
for i := 0; i < tickCount; i++ {
    processTick(i)
}
```

**Alternative patterns that cause the same bug:**

| Pattern | Buggy (off-by-one) | Fixed |
|---------|-------------------|-------|
| Loop start | `for i := 1; i <= n; i++` (n iterations, but wrong mapping) | `for i := 0; i < n; i++` |
| Slice ranging | `for range items[:n+1]` | `for range items[:n]` |
| Slice access | `items[i-1]` when i=0 causes panic | `items[i]` with proper bounds |
| Length check | `if len(items) >= n+1` | `if len(items) >= n` |
| Tick counting | `ticksProcessed == tickCount+1` | `ticksProcessed == tickCount` |

The fix is to ensure the self-test validates exactly **210 ticks** — not 209 and not 211 — by correcting the loop boundary or index expression.
